To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a heteroplasmatic variant of MTND1 gene was identified by WES in a West syndrome evolving to Lenox-Gastaut syndrome patient.
the mitochondrial MT- ND1 variant identified by WES was associated with complex I deficiency, which caused the epileptic encephalgia of the patient.

a novel mutation in the MTND1 gene is associated with WS evolving to Lennox Gastaut syndrome, and the pathomechanism involves complex I deficiency due to impaired protein stability and supercomplex formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the first description of the association of WS and the heteroplasmic mutation m.3946G > A in the MTND1 gene.
a new mutation in MTND1 gene that causes complex I deficiency in WS evolving to Lennox Gastaut syndrome.
a novel mutation (m.3947G>A) in the MTND1 gene associated to epileptic encephalcopathy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a heteroplasmia of m.3946G>A in the MT- ND1 gene causes complex I deficiency in patient fibroblast and this deficiency may lead to epileptic encephalcopathy.
the MT-NDI gene variant is the primary cause of the epileptic encephalcopathy in this patient.

this patient has a novel variant of the MTND1 gene that leads to WS with complex I deficiency and supercomplexes defects, and that the patient evolved to Lennox Gastaut syndrome due to the supercomplexes defect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MT-NDI gene mutation causes WS evolving to LGS through complex I deficiency and increased ROS production.
a heteroplasmically expressed variant in the MTND1 gene, p.E214 K, is responsible for the WS phenotype and its subsequent evolution into Lennox-Gastau syndrome (LGS).

the MT-NDI mutation identified here is a novel variant that is associated with complex I deficiency and epileptic encephalgia, which may be related to the pathogenesis of epileptiform discharges in the patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of WES in the context of a mitochondrial disease can be useful in identifying a pathogenic mutation in the mitochondrial genome.
WES is a powerful tool to identify the etiology of epileptic encephalgia with mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiency.
the use of WES data for whole mitochondrial DNA analysis is a valuable tool for the identification of variants associated with complex I deficiency.
